You write tests almost the same way as in Jest.
In ReelWalk it mainly tests the core package.
It checks that render job state transitions are correct.
It tests the decision to process or discard a queue message.
It also tests which file types can be uploaded.
The worker handler is tested with the database and S3 mocked.
CI runs every package through turbo run test.

why.point: Decision logic is split out into pure functions.
So it can be tested instantly without a database or queue.
But it cannot check real Chrome or SQS behaviour.
Playwright E2E covers that.

component.status: Real: Vitest suites in packages/core, packages/render and apps/worker run in CI's verify job on every push.

inRepo.file: Allowed transitions: happy path, retries, SUCCEEDED is final, the worker cannot be skipped.
decideDelivery (claim, duplicate, stale heartbeat), decideFailure exponential backoff, dead-letter handling.
Upload type resolution and object key rules.
handleDelivery and handleDeadLetter with vi.fn mocks: no double render, re-queue with backoff, DLQ on last attempt.

question.ask: What kind of unit tests did you write?
question.modelAnswer: The most important are the job state transition tests. They check that a succeeded job never leaves that state. A message delivered twice is not rendered twice. They also check that failures retry with exponential backoff.
question.whatTheyCheck: Tie it to idempotency: SQS is at-least-once, and the tests prove duplicates are harmless.

question.ask: What did you do to make the code easy to test?
question.modelAnswer: I separated decisions from side effects. decideDelivery only returns what to do. Database updates and S3 happen in the handler. The handler tests mock those with vi.fn.
question.whatTheyCheck: 'Functional core, imperative shell' is the idea; you don't need the English phrase, just the split.

question.ask: How do you divide work between unit tests and E2E?
question.modelAnswer: Logic combinations are covered by unit tests. They are fast, so I can write many cases. E2E covers only the important user flows. They are slow, so I keep them few.
question.whatTheyCheck: This is the test pyramid; mentioning it by name (テストピラミッド) is fine.

component.name: Playwright
component.oneLine: It tests user flows end to end in a real browser.

howItWorks.point: Playwright is a test tool that drives a browser automatically.
It operates the UI in a real Chromium.
ReelWalk is for phones, so tests run at a Pixel 7 viewport.
The main test makes a reel from photos and a video.
Then it really renders and checks the MP4 can be fetched.
A corrupt video tests failing after retries.
In CI, Docker Compose starts every service and the suite runs.
Locally, parallelism is set to 2.

why.point: Unit tests cannot check how the services connect.
E2E checks the whole path: web, queue, worker and S3.
The trade-off is that they are slow and prone to flakiness.
So CI retries once and keeps traces.

component.status: Real: the suite runs in CI against Docker Compose, including a real render to MP4; it can also point at the kind cluster via E2E_BASE_URL.

inRepo.file: Pixel 7 project, 5-minute timeout, 2 workers by default (the Windows 10 s stall note), 1 retry and traces on CI.
Create, edit and export a reel; Instagram limits; conflict between tabs; corrupt video fails then retries.
A file that passes upload checks but cannot be decoded, to drive the retry and DLQ path.

question.ask: What do your E2E tests check?
question.modelAnswer: They run user flows in the browser from start to finish. Making a reel, editing it and exporting it. The render is real: the worker produces an MP4. It checks the file is MP4 and larger than 50 KB. Failure cases use a corrupt video.
question.whatTheyCheck: Stress 'no mocks': the E2E goes through SQS (ElasticMQ), the worker, Chrome and S3 (MinIO).

question.ask: Why two workers locally?
question.modelAnswer: With five in parallel, requests stalled in exact 10-second steps. It happened even straight to MinIO, so it was not the app. It happened between the Windows host and Docker Desktop. Linux CI is unaffected, so only local runs use 2. The root cause is still under investigation.
question.whatTheyCheck: A good debugging story: you isolated the layer (原因の切り分け) before blaming the app. Don't claim a root cause you haven't found.

question.ask: How do you prevent flaky tests?
question.modelAnswer: Wait for state, not for a fixed time. For example, wait until data-status becomes SUCCEEDED. Elements are found by data-testid or role. CI retries once and keeps a trace on failure.
question.whatTheyCheck: Retries hide flakiness if overused; one retry plus a trace to investigate is a reasonable balance.

component.name: CloudFront
component.oneLine: A CDN that delivers finished videos quickly from a nearby edge.

howItWorks.point: CloudFront is AWS's CDN.
It can deliver video fast from edges around the world.
Today the app returns videos as S3 presigned URLs.
Setting an environment variable switches to CloudFront URLs.
In production the design keeps S3 private by using OAC.
Who can watch is controlled with signed URLs or signed cookies.
In production OAC is in place; signed URLs are not yet.

why.point: Videos are large, so serving straight from S3 is slower and costlier.
Each job's output key never changes, so it can be cached for a long time.
The trade-off is more setup: signing keys, OAC and so on.

component.status: Built: the production distribution (imported into Terraform, origin access control so only CloudFront reads the bucket) serves finished MP4s at dh5xvp6apljoh.cloudfront.net; the app uses it when CLOUDFRONT_BASE_URL is set and presigned S3 URLs otherwise. No signed URLs: share links are the access control.

inRepo.file: Early aws_cloudfront_distribution sketch in front of the media bucket.
mediaUrl: CloudFront when CLOUDFRONT_BASE_URL is set, otherwise a presigned GET.
Lists CloudFront among things kind does not cover.

question.ask: How do finished videos reach the user?
question.modelAnswer: Right now the app returns an S3 presigned URL. Locally MinIO stands in for S3. In production CloudFront delivers the finished videos. The share-link page uses those URLs too.
question.whatTheyCheck: CloudFront is real: the distribution was imported into Terraform with origin access control. What is not done is signed URLs; the share link is the access control today.

question.ask: How do OAC and signed URLs differ?
question.modelAnswer: OAC is CloudFront's permission to read S3. S3 stays private and only CloudFront can read it. A signed URL limits the viewer. It decides who can watch, and until when.
question.whatTheyCheck: They protect different hops: OAC is CloudFront to S3, signed URLs are viewer to CloudFront. Production would use both.

question.ask: How would you refresh the cache?
question.modelAnswer: The output key is built from the job ID. A succeeded job's video never changes. A new export means a new job and a new key. So invalidation is almost never needed.

component.name: Bedrock
component.oneLine: The plan is AI-drafted captions. It hasn't been built.

howItWorks.point: Bedrock is AWS's generative AI service.
You can call models such as Claude through an API.
ReelWalk has no AI features yet.
What I have in mind is drafting captions.
It would suggest Instagram text from the listing details.
I'd make the call from the worker, asynchronously.
The result is shown as a suggestion and always checked by a person.

why.point: Writing captions is a chore for real-estate agents.
With Bedrock, access is managed with IAM inside AWS.
But housing ads have strict wording rules, so review is a must.

component.status: Not built at all: there is no AI code or Bedrock call in the repo, only a one-line 'Bedrock captions are planned' note in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md; nothing beyond this outline is designed.

inRepo.file: Known gaps: 'No AI features yet (Bedrock captions are planned)'.
Caption limits a generated caption would have to pass.
Today's caption text comes from data per vibe, with the housing-ad rule.

question.ask: Do you already use AI features?
question.modelAnswer: No, not yet implemented. The idea is caption drafts. I lowered its priority and have not tried it yet.
question.whatTheyCheck: Answer 'no' cleanly first. An honest 未実装 followed by a sensible plan is far better than vagueness.

question.ask: If you added it, how would you wire it in?
question.modelAnswer: The same way as rendering: a queue and a worker. Model responses are slow, so the web request doesn't wait. I'd pass only the listing fields so it can't invent facts. The result also goes through the existing Instagram checks.

question.ask: How do you think about the risks of generative AI?
question.modelAnswer: The biggest is writing wrong facts about a property. Also, housing ads may not express a preference for who buys. So a person always reviews it before use. Cost is controlled with token limits.

component.name: CloudWatch
component.oneLine: Logs, metrics and alarms show how the system is doing.

howItWorks.point: CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring service.
Logs, metrics and alarms are in one place.
Today the worker logs to stdout with the job ID on each line.
On EKS the plan is to collect that in CloudWatch Logs.
The key metric is the age of the oldest message in the queue.
Any message in the DLQ raises an alarm right away.
I'd also like render time and failure rate as metrics.

why.point: When async work stalls, you don't notice it on screen right away.
So watching queue backlog and the DLQ gives the most value.
But more logs and metrics also means more cost.

component.status: Not wired up: web and worker log plain text to stdout and Kubernetes probes check health, but there is no CloudWatch agent, metric or alarm in the repo; everything CloudWatch-specific here is the plan.

inRepo.file: Log lines prefixed with [jobId] for each decision and attempt.
/healthz returns 503 if the poll loop stops ticking.
livenessProbe on /healthz; no readiness probe for a queue consumer.

question.ask: What would you monitor in production?
question.modelAnswer: First, the age of the oldest message in the queue. If it grows, workers are too few or stuck. Next, DLQ message count. Even one is an alarm. Then render failure rate and duration.
question.whatTheyCheck: ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage beats queue length: it shows user-facing delay directly.

question.ask: How would you notice a stuck worker?
question.modelAnswer: The worker has a health check endpoint. If the loop stops for a while, it returns 503. Then Kubernetes restarts it. The job is taken over by another pod after the timeout.
question.whatTheyCheck: This part is real and runs on kind. Separate it clearly from the CloudWatch alarms, which are only planned.

question.ask: How would you improve the logs?
question.modelAnswer: They are plain text now; I'd move to structured JSON. Job ID, generation and attempt become fields. Then CloudWatch can search and aggregate them.

component.name: IAM & Secrets
component.oneLine: Each workload gets only the permissions it needs, through a role.

howItWorks.point: AWS permissions are granted with IAM roles.
The rule is: no access keys inside containers.
On EKS, Pod Identity or IRSA attaches a role to a pod.
The web app only sends messages; the worker only receives and deletes.
That is the principle of least privilege.
The database password is passed in a Kubernetes Secret.
In production that Secret is managed outside the chart.
From CI to AWS, OIDC provides temporary credentials.

why.point: Long-lived keys do a lot of damage if they leak.
With roles, credentials rotate automatically.
However, the chart currently has a single ServiceAccount.
Splitting it between web and worker is the next improvement.

component.status: Built: CI assumes an IAM role through GitHub OIDC to push to ECR (no stored keys); on EKS pods used Pod Identity; on App Runner and Fargate the instance and task roles carry the same scoped policy; credentials sit in SSM Parameter Store. Locally the Secret holds throwaway MinIO and Postgres credentials.

inRepo.file: serviceAccount annotations for IRSA and secret.create / existingSecret.
The ConfigMap, the optional Secret and the shared ServiceAccount.
id-token: write and configure-aws-credentials with a role, skipped until configured.
ConfigMap vs Secret, and IRSA in production.

question.ask: What permissions would the worker get?
question.modelAnswer: Only receive, delete and change-visibility on the render queue. S3 is limited to reading and writing one bucket. Resources are named by ARN; wildcards are avoided. The web app gets only send and presigned-URL signing.
question.whatTheyCheck: Concrete actions (sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility) show you have thought it through. This policy is live: it is attached to the Fargate task role and the App Runner instance role.

question.ask: How do you manage secrets?
question.modelAnswer: On local kind, throwaway values go into a Secret. In production the design is that the chart doesn't create it. It would be synced from Secrets Manager with External Secrets. No secrets ever go into Git.

question.ask: What's the difference between IRSA and Pod Identity?
question.modelAnswer: Both give a pod an IAM role. IRSA uses an OIDC provider and an annotation on the SA. Pod Identity is newer and simpler to set up. For a new cluster I'd choose Pod Identity.
question.whatTheyCheck: The chart's comment mentions IRSA; either works. Saying you'd pick Pod Identity for new clusters shows current knowledge.

component.name: EKS
component.oneLine: AWS's managed Kubernetes service.

howItWorks.point: EKS stands for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service.
AWS runs the control plane and makes it redundant.
We can focus on the nodes and the app.
In ReelWalk, I ran the same Helm chart on EKS for a day.
Pods got AWS permissions through Pod Identity.
But most of the $250 a month was idle cost, so I retired it.
No static access keys.

why.point: Running the control plane yourself is hard work.
With EKS, availability and upgrades are handled by AWS.
On the other hand, the control plane alone costs money.
So the order is: verify on kind first, then move.

component.status: Built and retired: an EKS 1.34 cluster (Terraform, one t3.xlarge node, Pod Identity, RDS, ingress-nginx, cert-manager) ran reelwalking.com for one day on 2026-10-07 with a real render verified end to end, then was destroyed because it cost about $250 a month for an idle app (ADR 0014, superseded by ADR 0015).

inRepo.file: Why kind before EKS, and what only a real EKS cluster can prove.
Defaults for a real cluster: empty AWS endpoints, external Secret, the serviceAccount annotation slot for IRSA.

question.ask: Do you have experience running EKS?
question.modelAnswer: To be honest, I have not run EKS in production yet. My AWS account verification never completed, so I could not deploy. Instead, I verified the same chart on a local kind cluster. The EKS-specific differences are in values.yaml and the IRSA design. After joining I want to catch up quickly on real clusters.
question.whatTheyCheck: Do not bluff: the interviewer can probe node groups, upgrades and IRSA. An honest answer with a concrete plan scores better.

question.ask: How do pods get AWS permissions?
question.modelAnswer: The design uses IRSA. The ServiceAccount is annotated with an IAM role ARN. Pods automatically receive short-lived credentials. There is no need to put access keys into a Secret. values.yaml already has a slot for that.
question.whatTheyCheck: If they push further, mention EKS Pod Identity as the newer option, and least-privilege policies per workload.

question.ask: What would moving to EKS take?
question.modelAnswer: First, create the VPC, EKS, RDS and so on with Terraform. Then prepare a values file for EKS. CI pushes the images to ECR. The chart and application code should not need changes. But that is an untested hypothesis.
question.whatTheyCheck: ADR 0005 says exactly this: 'That claim is untested until it is done.'

term.ja: コントロールプレーン
ワーカーノード／ノードグループ

component.name: Terraform
component.oneLine: It defines and creates AWS resources as code.

howItWorks.point: Terraform is an IaC tool: infrastructure written as code.
You declare the desired state in a language called HCL.
plan shows the diff and apply makes the change.
ReelWalk defines S3, SQS and CloudFront.
RDS and ECS are written as placeholders too.
But it has never been applied.
It is an early draft, so it differs from the current design.

why.point: Manual setup can be neither reproduced nor reviewed.
As code, changes are reviewed in pull requests.
On the other hand, the state file must be managed safely.

component.status: Applied and live: remote state in S3 with lock files; the media bucket and CloudFront (imported), SQS with a DLQ, ECR, the GitHub OIDC role, the app IAM policy, a budget, the VPC, App Runner, the Fargate task definition and SSM parameters. EKS and RDS were created and destroyed the same day. CI scans infra/terraform with Trivy.

inRepo.file: S3 bucket, SQS queue (no DLQ yet), CloudFront in front of S3, and ECS/RDS/Redis placeholders.
Region, project and bucket name variables.
Notes that the Terraform started as an ECS/Fargate design before Kubernetes was chosen.

question.ask: What do you manage with Terraform?
question.modelAnswer: The S3 bucket and CloudFront for media, the SQS queues, ECR, and the IAM role for GitHub. Also the App Runner service, the Fargate task definition and the SSM parameters. State lives in S3; I check the plan diff before every apply. I also created EKS and RDS once, deleted them over cost, and recorded it in an ADR.
question.whatTheyCheck: It is live. Existing resources were imported, not recreated, so the CloudFront domain survived. The scanner findings (no WAF, no customer-managed key, public subnets) are accepted with reasons in .trivyignore.yaml.

question.ask: What are the problems with the current Terraform?
question.modelAnswer: It was written early, so it no longer matches the architecture. It has ECS and Redis, but we now use Kubernetes and no Redis. The SQS DLQ is not defined yet either. State is planned to live in S3 with locking. EKS and VPC definitions still need to be added.
question.whatTheyCheck: Self-critique is well received in Japanese interviews; it shows you know what 'done' looks like.

question.ask: How do you split responsibilities between Terraform and Helm?
question.modelAnswer: Terraform builds the AWS foundation. VPC, EKS, RDS, S3, SQS and so on. Helm deploys the app on top of it. They change at different rates, so they are managed separately.
question.whatTheyCheck: Lifecycle separation is the key idea: infrastructure changes rarely, the app changes every release.

question.ask: What are your strengths?
question.modelAnswer: My strength is understanding how things work before I build. In ReelWalk, I recorded why I use each technology in ADRs. For example, why I chose SQS and which options I rejected. So I can explain the reasoning behind a decision even later on.
question.whatTheyCheck: One strength, one piece of evidence they can check in the repo. Don't list three adjectives.

question.ask: What is your weakness?
question.modelAnswer: I sometimes dig too deep on my own. In ReelWalk, I spent too long investigating a delay that only happened locally. Now I set a time box and share progress partway through. In a team, asking early is faster overall.
question.whatTheyCheck: A real weakness plus what you now do about it. The 10 s stall is true: Playwright traces, then a 2-worker workaround instead of chasing it forever.

question.ask: Tell me about your experience developing in a team.
question.modelAnswer: At my previous job, I worked on 【what】 in a team of 【number】. We worked with 【process, e.g. a daily stand-up and two-week sprints】. What I paid attention to was making my progress visible early. 【One concrete episode】
question.whatTheyCheck: Their team is a PO plus three developers, works from documents and tickets, and checks the day's plan every morning. Mirror that if it is true for you.

question.ask: What do you pay attention to in code review?
question.modelAnswer: First, I check the change does what the description says. Next, I look at behaviour on errors and under concurrency. When I comment, I always give the reason and an alternative. Matters of taste I mark as "nit" so the author can decide. As an author, I keep pull requests small.
question.whatTheyCheck: The job post asks for someone who considers the other person (相手を慮る). Show you review the code, not the person.

question.ask: How do you choose technologies?
question.modelAnswer: First I pin down the problem and the constraints. Then I narrow it to two or three options and compare trade-offs. For the queue, for example, I compared Redis, PostgreSQL and SQS. I chose SQS because redelivery and a dead-letter queue come built in. I record the reasons as ADRs.
question.whatTheyCheck: At this company technology choices are the team's call, so they want people who can justify one. Mention a rejected option.

question.ask: Tell me about a failure and what you learned.
question.modelAnswer: In the first version, I passed jobs through a Redis list. When a worker crashed mid-job, the job was lost. The cause was that I'd assumed the queue would never fail. Since then I design assuming failures and duplicates will happen. Now it's handled with SQS and idempotent processing.
question.whatTheyCheck: Own the mistake in one line, spend the rest on the lesson. If you have a work example, use it instead and keep this one for the ReelWalk questions.

question.ask: What technology are you learning lately?
question.modelAnswer: Lately I've been focusing on Kubernetes. I ran a Helm chart on kind and set up probes and resource limits. I'm aiming for CKAD level, studying with 【method】. I've also experimented with Gaussian splatting for 3D property video.
question.whatTheyCheck: CKAD-level Kubernetes is a plus in the post. Name something you actually configured (readiness vs liveness is a good follow-up to be ready for).

question.ask: How do you handle a vulnerability?
question.modelAnswer: First I check which dependency is affected and where it's used. Then I set the priority from severity and whether it's actually exploitable. If there's a fix, I update and confirm with tests that nothing broke. If it can't be fixed right away, I accept it temporarily with a written reason. In ReelWalk, every Trivy exception has its reason written down. I've set up Dependabot to propose dependency updates weekly.
question.whatTheyCheck: This is a listed duty. Show a process (scope, exploitability, fix, verify, record), not just "I run npm audit".

question.ask: Is there anything you'd like to improve in CI/CD?
question.modelAnswer: First, the speed of feedback. Turborepo's cache can skip packages that haven't changed. Second, moving security checks earlier in the pipeline. Third, using Argo CD to keep production in line with what's in Git. But I'd want to hear your current pain points before setting priorities.
question.whatTheyCheck: CI/CD improvement is a listed duty. Offer ideas, then defer to their reality; proposing fixes before you know the pipeline sounds arrogant.

question.ask: What is your approach to testing?
question.modelAnswer: I pull logic out into pure functions and test them with Vitest. For example, job state transitions and retry decisions. User flows are checked in a real browser with Playwright. The end-to-end tests go as far as actually rendering a video. End-to-end tests are slow, so most of the tests are unit tests.
question.whatTheyCheck: Their stack is Vitest plus Playwright, the same split. Mention the test pyramid without using jargon for its own sake.

question.ask: Why do you want to work in Japan?
question.modelAnswer: I became interested in Japan through 【your connection, e.g. study or work】. I respect how carefully Japanese teams approach quality. I felt the same in your phrase "build software with integrity." 【Your situation or plans for living in Japan】 I want to work in Japan for the long term and grow as an engineer.
question.whatTheyCheck: They want to know you will stay. Be concrete about visa, location and timeline if asked; keep it positive about Japan, not negative about home.

question.ask: Are you worried about working in Japanese?
question.modelAnswer: I can handle technical conversations if they're not too fast. My reading and writing are at JLPT N2 level. When I don't know a word, I check it on the spot. I find important decisions are safest written down in tickets or chat. Every day I improve my work Japanese through 【method】.
question.whatTheyCheck: This whole interview is the answer. Be honest about the level, show a strategy; their team works from documents and tickets, which helps you.

question.ask: What would you like to do after joining?
question.modelAnswer: First, I want to understand the shipping tool's code and its business. I'd start with small changes and bug fixes and ship something early. After that I'd like to work on improving CI/CD and vulnerability handling. Eventually I want to be trusted with both the app and the infrastructure.
question.whatTheyCheck: Show a ramp: learn, ship small, then improve. Naming their product shows you read the post.

question.ask: How do you use AI tools?
question.modelAnswer: I use AI coding agents every day. I built ReelWalk together with Claude Code too. But I make the design decisions myself and record the reasons in ADRs. I always check generated code with tests and review. I also follow rules on usage, like never pasting secrets.
question.whatTheyCheck: The company promotes AI use, and the public repo shows AI co-authored commits, so be open about it. The point to land: you own the decisions and can explain every part.

question.ask: What do you do when the team disagrees?
question.modelAnswer: First I ask about the reasoning behind the other view. Usually it's just different assumptions or priorities. Once we agree on criteria, we compare with a small experiment. Once it's decided, I commit fully even if it wasn't my idea.
question.whatTheyCheck: Value: チームで価値を最大化する. They are checking cooperation, not who wins.

question.ask: Why are you looking for a new job?
question.modelAnswer: 【One positive line about your current or last job】 Along the way, I came to want to work on both the app and the infrastructure. Building ReelWalk, I found Kubernetes and CI/CD especially interesting. I want to apply that on a real product, with a real team.
question.whatTheyCheck: Never criticise a previous employer. Frame it as moving toward something they offer.

question.ask: Are you stronger in frontend or backend?
question.modelAnswer: In terms of experience, I've done more 【frontend / backend】. But in ReelWalk I built both myself. Autosave, for example, spans both the screen and the server. Saves based on an old revision are rejected, so a second tab can't overwrite the first. More than either side, I enjoy designing the boundary between them.
question.whatTheyCheck: Full-stack roles want someone comfortable at the seam. The revision check (ADR 0006) is a good concrete example.

question.ask: How do you respond to a production incident?
question.modelAnswer: First I check the impact and tell the people affected. Then I stop the user impact with a quick mitigation. Once things are stable, I find the root cause from the logs. Finally we agree on prevention and write up a retrospective. 【One line from a real incident, if you have one】
question.whatTheyCheck: Order matters: communicate, mitigate, then investigate. Don't claim on-call experience you don't have.

question.ask: Is working in the office OK for you?
question.modelAnswer: Yes, no problem. 【Where you live and the commute to Kanda】 Sitting close makes it easy to ask questions, so I think it suits me.
question.whatTheyCheck: The post asks for office work at the Kanda office, and says the team sits close and talks as needed.
